doc.title: Tommy Newsom and Ross Tompkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Advice for students and jazz education
summary: Opportunities are harder than before, though jazz is now taught in colleges and the service bands are strong.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well do you gentlemen have any words of wisdom for our students who might watch this who want to be professional musicians? Besides don’t quit your day gig?
Well, there’s always a way if you’re, if you want it badly enough, you’re going to get it. It’s probably more difficult now than it was when we were younger.
Yeah, well I think the opportunities —
Who can you go on the road with now? Count Basie is the only band left. And that’s not Basie of course it’s a ghost band.
Well there’s still the Tommy Dorsey band and there’s maybe a Woody Herman band.
I think that’s part time. I don’t think the guy does it all the time or something. But there’s not much of a choice. But of course now you can go to almost any college and study jazz,
which there was no such thing as that. He couldn’t even bring his saxophone in to Peabody.
Yeah. Actually the college bands are, there’s a lot of dynamite college bands, some of the best I’ve heard.
I guess the most famous one is down there in Texas, that’s probably the oldest one.
The two original students at that school in the 40s were Jimmy Giuffre and Herb Ellis.
Is that right? I didn’t know that.
They were the two guys that started off that went to that college.
By golly. Yeah they have a hell of a record. So that, and there are several dynamite service bands.
